Chapter 20 · Expansion · 1896–hoy

Psychotherapies and professionalisation

From Witmer's first psychological clinic to cognitive behavioural therapy, Spain's PIR residency and evidence-based psychology.

For its first decades psychology was mainly a university discipline. Its transformation into a health profession, with degrees, professional bodies and evaluated treatments, is a twentieth-century story that has had its own milestones in Spain.

What were people trying to understand?

Which psychological treatments work, for which problems and under what conditions; how to train practitioners and how to assure the public that someone offering therapy is qualified to do so.

With what methods?

At first, clinical experience. Then, increasingly, controlled trials and meta-analyses. In 1896 Lightner Witmer opened the first psychological clinic at the University of Pennsylvania, for children with learning difficulties, and coined the term "clinical psychology". In 1952 Hans Eysenck published a provocative review arguing that psychotherapy did not improve outcomes beyond spontaneous recovery. His data were questionable, but he forced the profession to demonstrate its effectiveness. In 1977 Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass pooled hundreds of studies in one of the first meta-analyses in history and concluded that therapy did work.

Who took part?

In 1949 the Boulder conference in Colorado defined the scientist-practitioner model: clinical psychologists should be trained both as researchers and as therapists. Joseph Wolpe developed systematic desensitisation for phobias in 1958. Albert Ellis proposed rational emotive therapy from 1955 and Aaron T. Beck cognitive therapy for depression in the 1960s: both held that the way we interpret events shapes our emotions. Cognitive behavioural therapy grew out of the union of these currents with behaviourism. Later came the "third-wave" therapies, such as Marsha Linehan's dialectical behaviour therapy and acceptance and commitment therapy.

In Spain, the degree in psychology began in 1968 as a specialisation within philosophy in Madrid and Barcelona. The Official College of Psychologists was created by law in 1979. In 1993 the first PIR (Psicólogo Interno Residente) residency places were offered, the equivalent of the medical MIR, and the specialty of Clinical Psychology was regulated in 1998. In 2011 the qualification of general health psychologist was created, with a master's degree that grants the licence to practise.

What did it contribute?

  • Psychological treatments with demonstrated efficacy for depression, anxiety, insomnia, chronic pain and many other problems.
  • Clinical guidelines, such as those of the UK's NICE, that recommend psychotherapy as the first option for several disorders.
  • A regulated profession, with formal training and a code of ethics.
  • Collaboration between psychology, family medicine and psychiatry in health care.

What was revised later?

The debate over what makes a therapy work is still open. Many studies find similar results between different well-delivered approaches, which points to the importance of common factors such as the therapeutic alliance. Lists of empirically supported treatments have been criticised for relying on trials with highly selected patients. And in many countries, Spain included, access to psychotherapy in public health care still falls short of real demand, with long waiting lists, a problem the profession and governments are still trying to solve.

In primary care, a substantial share of consultations is estimated to have an emotional component. That is why several countries have tried models with psychologists working inside health centres, with promising results.
